Messages.Author: Jamie The Seppo
Messages.Body:
Yello,
I was wondering about the Continental Championships and the
qualifing. Can someone give up their qualifing spot to someone (or at
least to the next person down the line) at a Qualifier?
If so, are there any other guidelines about the procedure?

Danke
Jamie
The Seppo

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


Any player can decide not to be counted for the qualifying spots.
That player must inform the judge before the tournament begins
(before the first round starts) that she does not wish to be
counted for qualification purposes.
That player is then treated exactly as a pre-qualified player
would be (for the purposes of that tournament, that is).

Makes sense. But that means that the "you can declare you're not
intending to go to the championships" option isn't likely to actually
help Australian players all that much in improving their ability to get
the geographically distant qualifying players to their continental
championship tournament.

Of course, the rule may not have been intended specifically to be of use
to Australian players. But in this case, perhaps they could use some
other help (eg continent-specific qualifying rules, rather than the same
qualifying rules as the other three organized continents, as it seems
clear that each continent has enough unique characteristics that one
approach does not necessarily fit all).

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
In message <bv63gh$p3taj$1...@ID-121616.news.uni-berlin.de>,
"Joshua Duffin" <jtdu...@yahoo.com> mumbled something about:

>to Australian players. But in this case, perhaps they could use some
>other help (eg continent-specific qualifying rules, rather than the same
>qualifying rules as the other three organized continents, as it seems
>clear that each continent has enough unique characteristics that one
>approach does not necessarily fit all).

God forbid that I should provide assistance of a positive nature...

I suggest that all players who make the Final Table of a qualifier could
be automatically qualified, regardless of 25% considerations, and the
25% be extended from there. This rule would apply to all continents.

Benefits:

1) Solves problem stated above, where 15 "i ain't goings" produce 1.25
qualifying positions available in a 20-person tournament. Untidy.

2) Easily extensible with 25% rule. Assume 30-person tournament in
order to make math more difficult. 15 players declare intent to not
qualify, leaving 4 qualifying positions available (25% of 15, rounded
up). Two of those players make the final table. 3 others from final
qualify, next 1 down the chain qualifies. OK, maybe not even that
complicated, but you get the idea.

3) Solves problem of having final potentially become one HUGE
out-of-game consideration, especially if less qualifying spots than
finalists. If there are only 4 spots, only the person who sat 5th has
any incentive whatsoever to do anything but wall up and defend for 2
hours, taking the timeout, and qualifying by default.

Saying that "you should play to win" is all well and good, but it won't
happen when it comes down to the wire -- people will have their eye on
the qualifier spots and will rationalize their decisions away
accordingly. It is entirely possible in the above scenario that 4
people would immediately jump on the weakest player and oust him/her,
even cross table -- which doesn't even violate the play to win rule
since you don't give up the Game Win.

Drawbacks:

1) Mandatory minimum size for tournaments to be considered qualifier
might be necessary. 5 players qualifying from 12-person tournament is
only 2 more than 25% but still might be too much?

2) More complex than original rule, and is not relevant for tournaments
with 20 or more non-eligible players anyway. To quote from Chief
Herman's Holiday Fun Pack: is this adding on too much clay?

3) Overenthusiasm might lead to people wanting the top 5 eligible
players to be qualified no matter what, potentially leading back around
to the "all but 2 eligible players qualified" syndrome. OK, sure that's
a bit of a stretch, but just a thought.

Discussion?

-- Derek
